standfirst: A small town with a twenty-year-old unsolved case, a detective everybody suspects, and the young officer sent to watch him. It is one of the best-written K-dramas ever made. One caveat up front: it should have been ten episodes rather than sixteen. Episodes one to eight ask whether he did it. Nine to sixteen answer a completely different question, and that pivot is the whole show.

picks.why: The obvious pairing, and the correct one. A prosecutor who feels nothing and a detective who feels everything, a case that keeps widening into the institution around it, and a script so tight that no scene is decoration. Same faith in silence and in the viewer's attention. Difference: it never asks you to doubt its own leads, so you lose the specific queasiness of not knowing whose side you are on.

For the second half rather than the first. Criminal profilers doing quiet, unglamorous work, a script interested in what proximity to violence does to the people who study it, and a lead performance built almost entirely out of listening. It answers the question Beyond Evil circles: what is a monster, and who gets to decide. Difference: episodic and undramatic by design. No town, no partnership, no cliffhangers.

Watch this one next, or first if you have not. Cold cases worked across time, a partnership built on trust that keeps getting tested, and consequences that arrive out of order and hurt. Difference: it has a fantasy device and a much faster pulse. Where Beyond Evil sits in a room for ten minutes, this cuts.

The standard pairing in both directions, with one caveat: if Mouse is your favourite of the two then Beyond Evil plays slow, and if Beyond Evil is then Mouse plays over the top. Same central question about whether evil is born. Difference: it is a plot machine with a mid-series identity change, willing to be lurid where Beyond Evil is restrained.

For the sustained not-knowing. A man with a false name, someone who loves him closing in, and the same interest in what maintaining a lie costs the liar. Difference: it is a marriage story underneath, so it is warmer and more conventional, and it chooses hope where Beyond Evil chooses reckoning.

For the provincial precinct texture. A modern detective stuck among police who do things the old way, older crimes that were never properly worked, and a growing suspicion that the institution was the problem all along. Difference: there is a fantasy premise and a comic streak, and the ending is a genuine coin flip on whether it satisfies you.

against.title: Vagabond
against.why: Lands in the same lists because it is filed under Korean thriller, which is not the same as being a match. It is a big-budget espionage action series with chases and set pieces, and it ends on an unresolved hook. Beyond Evil is two men talking in a fish shop. Nothing about the pleasure transfers.

against.title: Voice
against.why: Suggested for the serial-killer overlap. Voice is an adrenaline procedural built on emergency calls and a killer per season, engineered for pace. Beyond Evil's entire method is withholding. If you liked being made to wait, this will feel like being shouted at.

against.title: Tell Me What You Saw
against.why: The other cerebral Korean profiler thriller with a reclusive genius, and the resemblance stops at the logline. It is a puzzle show with a supervillain, and the satisfaction is watching a brilliant man be right. Beyond Evil is about two ordinary men being wrong about each other for eight hours.
